content.text:
1.1 A Lakh Varieties!
Eshwarappa is a farmer in Chintamani, a town in Karnataka. He visits the market regularly to buy seeds for his rice field. During one such visit he overheard a conversation between Ramanna and Lakshmamma. Ramanna said, "Earlier our country had about a lakh varieties of rice. Farmers used to preserve different varieties of seeds and use them to grow rice. Now, we only have a handful of varieties. Also, farmers have to come to the market to buy seeds".
Lakshmamma said, "There is a seed bank near my house. So far, they have collected about a hundred indigenous varieties of rice seeds from different places. You can also buy seeds from there."
You may have heard the word 'lakh' before. Do you know how big one lakh is? Let us find out.
Eshwarappa shared this incident with his daughter Roxie and son Estu.
Estu was surprised to know that there were about one lakh varieties of rice in this country. He wondered "One lakh! So far I have only tasted 3 varieties. If we tried a new variety each day, would we even come close to tasting all the varieties in a lifetime of 100 years?"
What do you think? Guess.

media.title: Lakh Ruler
media.context: Class 7 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 1 'Large Numbers Around Us' (A Lakh and Reading Large Numbers). Place a number on the ruler. How far is it from one lakh? Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Lakh Ruler. Place a number on the ruler. How far is it from one lakh? Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: A number can be placed on a ruler marked at one lakh; the gap to the mark is found by subtracting the smaller from the larger, and the change between two numbers is the larger minus the smaller.
tool_config.title: Lakh Ruler
tool_config.screen: A horizontal ruler from 0 to 2,00,000 with a bold mark at 1,00,000; a draggable pointer with a number box; a gap bar that grows between the pointer and the mark and says less than or more than one lakh; a second pointer for finding the change between two numbers.
feedback: A wrong gap shows the subtraction with the larger number first, so the order is clear.
A pointer on the wrong side of the mark turns the gap bar to the other colour and names less than or more than.
A correct answer shows the subtraction in a line, for example 1,00,000 minus 75,000.
tool_config.done_when: All six placements are done with the right gap or change.
challenges: Place 75,000 and find how much less than one lakh it is (25,000).
Place 1,06,000 and find how much more than one lakh it is (6,000).
Place both and find the change from 75,000 to 1,06,000 (31,000).
Place 99,500 and find the gap to one lakh (500).
Place 1,25,000 and find the gap to one lakh (25,000).
Place 36,500 and 1,09,500 and find which is closer to one lakh (1,09,500, gap 9,500).

hint_ladder.text: Is the number to the left or to the right of the one lakh mark?
The gap is the larger number minus the smaller number.
Subtract the number on the left of the mark from 1,00,000, or 1,00,000 from the number on the right.
The subtraction is shown with the answer, and a new number follows.

Read the gap bar and type how far the number is from one lakh.
Add a second pointer and type the change between the two numbers.
Press Check to see the subtraction written out.

But how much is one lakh? Observe the pattern and fill in the boxes given below.
The largest 3-digit number is 999. The smallest 4-digit number is __. The largest 4-digit number is __. The smallest 5-digit number is __. The largest 5-digit number is __. The smallest 6-digit number is 1,00,000.
99,995, 99,996, 99,998 ... each step is +1.
1,00,000 is read as "One Lakh".

content.text:
Roxie and Estu found that if they ate one variety of rice a day, they would come nowhere close to a lakh in a lifetime! Roxie suggests, "What if we ate 2 varieties of rice every day? Would we then be able to eat 1 lakh varieties of rice in 100 years?"
What if a person ate 3 varieties of rice every day? Will they be able to taste all the lakh varieties in a 100 year lifetime? Find out.
Estu said, "We know how many days there are in a year, 365, if we ignore leap years. If we live for y years, the number of days in our lifetime will be 365 × y."
Choose a number for y. How close to one lakh is the number of days in y years, for the y of your choice?

To see how far a number is below one lakh, subtract it from 1,00,000.
To see how far it is above one lakh, subtract 1,00,000 from it.
The change between two numbers is the larger one minus the smaller one.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M1.S3.T3.C7.IMG1}}
$1$. $999 + 1 = 1000$, the smallest $4$-digit number.
$2$. The largest $4$-digit number is $9999$.
$3$. $9999 + 1 = 10,000$, the smallest $5$-digit number.

content.text:
$1$. Days in $100$ years: $365 \times 100 = 36,500$.
$2$. One a day: $36,500$ varieties.
$3$. Two a day: $36,500 \times 2 = 73,000$ varieties.
$4$. Three a day: $36,500 \times 3 = 1,09,500$ varieties.
$5$. $1,00,000 - 73,000 = 27,000$, so two a day falls short of one lakh.
$6$. $1,09,500 - 1,00,000 = 9,500$, so three a day passes one lakh.
Answer: $36,500$; $73,000$; $1,09,500$. Only three varieties a day passes one lakh.

media.generation_prompt:
MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Show how a 1 metre person and a 4 metre floor build up the 40 metre height of a ten floor building.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a middle-school maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: #009E73 for a positive/first idea, #D55E00 for a negative/contrasting idea, #0072B2 for a first set or step, #E69F00 for a second set or step, #CC79A7 for the focus or highlight, #6B7280 for construction lines and for anything struck out. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Keep it uncluttered: one main idea per frame, a single clear focal object, generous white space around it, large readable labels, nothing decorative that does not teach. A tall building of stacked floors on the right, a small Somu figure on the left at the base, with one bracket on each side; white space around.

Exact mathematical structure:
- A building drawn as 10 equal stacked rectangles (floors) in one column, outlined #2B2B2B, alternating teal #0072B2 and amber #E69F00 fills, on a flat grey #6B7280 ground line.
- On the left of the building at ground level one simple flat Somu figure (no face), reddish purple #CC79A7, with a small vertical bracket beside him labelled '1 m'.
- A grey bracket beside the bottom floor only, labelled '1 floor = 4 m' (equal to 4 Somus).
- A grey bracket on the right spanning all 10 floors labelled '10 floors = 40 m'.
- Exactly 10 floors, bottom floor the same height as 4 Somu figures stacked.

Visible text:
- 1 m
- 1 floor = 4 m
- 10 floors = 40 m

Critical rejection conditions:
- floor count other than 10
- bottom floor not four times the height of Somu
- any statue, waterfall or other height drawn
- any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number

Student takeaway: One floor is 4 m, so 10 floors make 40 m.

topics.summary: A large number becomes easier to feel when it is compared with something familiar; one lakh is big or small depending on what it is compared with.

content.text:
Getting a Feel of Large Numbers
You may have come across interesting facts like these:
The world's tallest statue is the 'Statue of Unity' in Gujarat depicting Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Its height is about 180 metres.
Kunchikal waterfall in Karnataka is said to drop from a height of about 450 metres.
It is not always easy to get a sense of how big these measurements are. But, we can get a better sense of their size when we compare them with something familiar. Let us see an example.
Look at the picture on the right. Somu is 1 metre tall. If each floor is about four times his height, what is the approximate height of the building?
Which is taller, The Statue of Unity or this building? How much taller?
We can see that the height of the Statue of Unity is close to 4 times the height of Somu's building.
How much taller is the Kunchikal waterfall than Somu's building?
How many floors should Somu's building have to be as high as the waterfall?

1. The picture shows Somu, 1 metre tall, standing beside a building of 10 floors. One floor is about as tall as four Somus.

content.text:
Is One Lakh a Very Large Number?
Eshwarappa asked Roxie and Estu, "Is a lakh big or small?"
Roxie feels that 1 lakh is a large number: "We had one lakh varieties of rice, that is a lot." "Living 1 lakh days would mean living for 274 years, that is a really long time!" "If 1 lakh people stood shoulder to shoulder in a line they could stretch as far as 38 kilometres."
Estu, however, thinks it is not that big: "Do you know that the cricket stadium in Ahmedabad has a seating capacity of more than 1 lakh? One lakh people in such a small area!" "Most humans have 80,000 to 1,20,000 hairs on their heads. Imagine, 1 lakh hairs fit in such a tiny space!" "I heard that there are some species of fish where a female fish can lay almost one lakh eggs at once very comfortably. Some even lay tens of lakhs of eggs at a time."
How do you view a lakh, is a lakh big or small?
Note to the Teacher: Encourage students to make connections between these facts. For example, can the whole population of Chintamani fit in the stadium? How can we imagine the line of 38 km, having a lakh people, sitting next to each other in the stadium?

content.text:
Worked example: Check Roxie's two claims: 1 lakh days is about 274 years, and 1 lakh people shoulder to shoulder stretch about 38 km. Assume a person is 38 cm wide. Is a lakh big or small?
1. Years in 1 lakh days: 1,00,000 ÷ 365 is about 274 years.
2. Line of people: 1,00,000 × 38 = 38,00,000 cm.
3. 38,00,000 ÷ 100 = 38,000 m, and 38,000 ÷ 1000 = 38 km.
4. Both claims hold, so a lakh days and a lakh people in a row are long.
5. A lakh seats in a stadium or a lakh hairs on a head fit in a small space, so a lakh can look small.
6. So a lakh is big or small depending on what it is compared with.
Answer: About 274 years and 38 km; a lakh is big or small depending on the comparison

concepts.concept_name: Getting a Feel for Large Numbers: Q1

content.text:
$1$. One floor is $4 \times 1 = 4\text{ m}$, so $10$ floors are $10 \times 4 = 40\text{ m}$.
$2$. Statue of Unity: $180 - 40 = 140\text{ m}$ taller than the building.
$3$. Kunchikal waterfall: $450 - 40 = 410\text{ m}$ taller than the building.
$4$. Floors for $450\text{ m}$: $450 \div 4$ is $112.5$, so about $113$ floors.
$5$. The statue is $180 \div 40 = 4.5$ times the building, a little more than $4$ times.
Answer: The building is $40\text{ m}$; the statue is $140\text{ m}$ taller; the waterfall is $410\text{ m}$ taller; about $113$ floors
steps: One floor is 4 × 1 = 4 m, so 10 floors are 10 × 4 = 40 m.

Kunchikal waterfall: 450 − 40 = 410 m taller than the building.
Floors for 450 m: 450 ÷ 4 is 112.5, so about 113 floors.
The statue is 180 ÷ 40 = 4.5 times the building, a little more than 4 times.

content.text:
Reading and Writing Numbers
We have already been using commas for 5-digit numbers like 45,830 in the Indian place value system. As numbers grow bigger, using commas helps in reading the numbers easily. We use a comma in between the digits representing the "ten thousands" place and the "one lakh" place as you have seen just before (1,00,000).
The number name of 12,78,830 is twelve lakh seventy eight thousand eight hundred thirty. Similarly, the number 15,75,000 in words is fifteen lakh seventy five thousand.
Write each of the numbers given below in words: (a) 3,00,600 (b) 5,04,085 (c) 27,30,000 (d) 70,53,138

beats.on_screen: To find: the presses for each number; the number shown by 582 presses; is the claim true?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, divide each number by one hundred.
Four hundred needs four presses, and three thousand seven hundred needs thirty seven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ten thousand needs one hundred presses.
We divide because each press adds exactly one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, fifty three thousand needs five hundred thirty presses, and ninety thousand needs nine hundred.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ninety seven thousand six hundred needs nine hundred seventy six presses.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>One lakh needs one thousand presses.
We divide again, so the same rule gives every number of presses.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, five hundred eighty two presses add five hundred eighty two hundreds.
That is fifty eight thousand two hundred.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ten thousand holds one hundred hundreds, and one lakh holds one thousand hundreds.
We multiply because each of the presses adds one hundred.

media.title: Trading Board
media.context: Class 7 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 1 'Large Numbers Around Us' (The Land of Tens and Calculators). Press buttons. Trade counters. One number, many ways. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Trading Board. Press buttons. Trade counters. One number, many ways. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: Ten presses of a button can be traded for one press of the next bigger button, so the same number can be made in many ways, and every way gives an expression that adds to the number.
tool_config.title: Trading Board
tool_config.screen: A board with columns for the buttons plus one, plus ten, plus hundred, plus thousand, plus ten thousand and plus lakh; counters in each column; a trade arrow between neighbouring columns; an expression line that updates as counters move; a total box that must match the target.
feedback: A trade that is not ten for one is refused with the exchange rate shown.
A total that does not match the target is highlighted with how far it is.
A correct way is added to a list of ways with its expression and its press count.
tool_config.done_when: Two different ways with correct expressions are found for each of the six numbers.
challenges: 8300 in two ways (8 thousands and 3 hundreds, or 83 hundreds).
997 using 34 presses (trade one hundred for ten tens).

hint_ladder.text: Which button has the biggest value that fits into the target?
Trade one counter for ten counters of the next smaller button.
Check that the expression still adds to the target.
One trade is done for you and the expression is shown; a new number follows.

student_does: Predict how many presses each button needs to reach the target.
Place counters in the columns to reach the target.
Trade one counter for ten in the column to its right, or ten for one in the column to its left.
Read the expression line and press Check to confirm it adds to the target.

content.text:
$1$. Start from $5072 = 5000 + 70 + 2$.
$2$. Use $4$ presses of $+1000$ and trade the last $1000$ for $10$ presses of $+100$.
$3$. $(4 \times 1000) + (10 \times 100) + (7 \times 10) + (2 \times 1) = 4000 + 1000 + 70 + 2 = 5072$.
$4$. That is $4 + 10 + 7 + 2 = 23$ presses; the sum is $5072$, so the way works.
Answer: $(4 \times 1000) + (10 \times 100) + (7 \times 10) + (2 \times 1) = 5072$

content.text: $997$ can be made with $25$ presses. Make $997$ with a different number of presses. Then find the largest and the smallest $3$-digit number that can be made with exactly $30$ presses.

content.publication_text: $997$ can be made with $25$ presses. Make $997$ with a different number of presses. Then find the largest and the smallest $3$-digit number that can be made with exactly $30$ presses.

content.text:
$1$. $997 = (9 \times 100) + (9 \times 10) + (7 \times 1)$ takes $9 + 9 + 7 = 25$ presses.
$2$. Trade one $+100$ press for ten $+10$ presses: $(8 \times 100) + (19 \times 10) + (7 \times 1) = 997$.
$3$. That takes $8 + 19 + 7 = 34$ presses, nine more than before.
$4$. For $30$ presses the digit sum must be $30 - 9 = 21$ or $30 - 18 = 12$ or $3$, since each trade adds $9$.
$5$. Largest $3$-digit number: $993$, with the digit sum $21$: $(8 \times 100) + (19 \times 10) + (3 \times 1) = 993$ uses $8 + 19 + 3 = 30$ presses.
$6$. Smallest $3$-digit number: $102$, with the digit sum $3$: $(8 \times 10) + (22 \times 1) = 102$ uses $8 + 22 = 30$ presses.
Answer: $997$ in $34$ presses too; largest $993$ and smallest $102$ with exactly $30$ presses

content.text:
Systematic Sippy is a different kind of calculator. It has the following buttons: +1, +10, +100, +1000, +10000, +100000. It wants to be used as minimally as possible.
How can we get the numbers (a) 5072, (b) 8300 using as few button clicks as possible? Find out which buttons should be clicked and how many times to get the desired numbers given in the table. The aim is to click as few buttons as possible.
Here is one way to get the number 5072. This method uses 23 button clicks in total.
Is there another way to get 5072 using less than 23 button clicks? Write the expression for the same.

content.publication_text:
Systematic Sippy is a different kind of calculator. It has the following buttons: +1, +10, +100, +1000, +10000, +100000. It wants to be used as minimally as possible.
How can we get the numbers (a) 5072, (b) 8300 using as few button clicks as possible? Find out which buttons should be clicked and how many times to get the desired numbers given in the table. The aim is to click as few buttons as possible.
Here is one way to get the number 5072. This method uses 23 button clicks in total.
Is there another way to get 5072 using less than 23 button clicks? Write the expression for the same.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 5072 made with 5 presses of +1000, 6 of +10 and 12 of +1 takes 23 presses. Can it be done in fewer?
2. Ten presses of one button can always be traded for one press of the next bigger button, which saves nine presses.
3. So every button except the biggest is pressed at most nine times: the presses are the digits.

content.text:
What if we press the +10,00,000 button ten times? What number will come up? How many zeroes will it have? What should we call it?
The number will be 100 lakhs, which is also called a crore. 1 crore is written as 1,00,00,000, it is 1 followed by seven zeroes.

content.text:
Worked example: Press the +10,00,000 button ten times. What number appears, how many zeros does it have, and what is it called?
1. Ten presses: 10 × 10,00,000 = 1,00,00,000.
2. 10 lakhs ten times is 100 lakhs.
3. Count the zeros in 1,00,00,000: there are seven.
4. 100 lakhs is called one crore.
Answer: 1,00,00,000, which is 100 lakhs, 1 followed by seven zeros, called a crore

content.text:
The digits of a number are the fewest presses for each place.
The fewest presses equal the sum of the digits.
Ten presses of a button are never needed because one press of the next button does the same.

content.text:
$1$. $(a)$: $5072 = (5 \times 1000) + (0 \times 100) + (7 \times 10) + (2 \times 1)$: the presses are the digits $5$, $0$, $7$ and $2$.
$2$. Number of presses: $5 + 7 + 2 = 14$, which is fewer than $23$.
$3$. $(b)$: $8300 = (8 \times 1000) + (3 \times 100)$.
$4$. Number of presses: $8 + 3 = 11$.
Answer: $(a)$: $(5 \times 1000) + (7 \times 10) + (2 \times 1)$ in $14$ presses; $(b)$: $(8 \times 1000) + (3 \times 100)$ in $11$ presses

content.text: Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?
content.question: Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?
content.question_tex: Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?

content.text:
$1$. Take the number $8300$: its digits are $8$, $3$, $0$ and $0$, and $8 + 3 + 0 + 0 = 11$ is its smallest number of clicks.
$2$. $40629$ has digits adding to $4 + 0 + 6 + 2 + 9 = 21$, the smallest clicks.
$3$. $56354$ gives $5 + 6 + 3 + 5 + 4 = 23$, and $66666$ gives $6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 30$.
$4$. $367813$ gives $3 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 1 + 3 = 28$.
$5$. So the smallest number of clicks is the sum of the digits of the number.
Answer: The smallest number of clicks is the sum of the digits of the number

content.text:
$1$. Ten presses of one button make the same amount as one press of the next bigger button.
$2$. So in the fewest way no button other than the biggest is pressed ten or more times.
$3$. Each press count is then a single digit from $0$ to $9$, written in that button's place.
$4$. Written side by side, these counts are the digits of the number in place value notation, for example $5072$ has $5$ thousands, $0$ hundreds, $7$ tens and $2$ ones.
Answer: Each place holds at most nine presses, so the counts are the digits of the number

media.description: System Converter. One number, two ways to write it. Group it, name it, convert it. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. content.text:
1.3 Of Crores and Crores!
The table below shows some numbers according to both the Indian system and the American system (also called the International system) of naming numerals and placing commas. Observe the placement of commas in both systems.
Indian system: 1,000 One thousand; 10,000 Ten thousand; 1,00,000 One lakh; 10,00,000 Ten lakhs; 1,00,00,000 One crore; 10,00,00,000 Ten crores; 1,00,00,00,000 One arab or One hundred crores.
American system: 1,000 One thousand; 10,000 Ten thousand; 100,000 Hundred thousand; 1,000,000 One million; 10,000,000 Ten million; 100,000,000 Hundred million; 1,000,000,000 One billion.
Notice that in the Indian system, commas are placed to group the digits in a 3-2-2-2... pattern from right to left (thousands, lakhs, crores, etc.). In the American system, the digits are grouped uniformly in a 3-3-3-3... pattern from right to left (thousands, millions, billions, etc.).
The Indian system of naming numbers is also followed in Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Maldives, Afghanistan, and Myanmar. The words lakh and crore originate from the Sanskrit words lakṣha and koṭi. The American system is also used in many countries.

content.text:
Worked example: Place commas in 12345678 in the Indian and the American system and read it in both.
1. Indian system, groups of 3 then 2s: the last three digits 678, then 45, then 23, then 1.
2. So 12345678 is 1,23,45,678: one crore twenty three lakh forty five thousand six hundred seventy eight.
3. American system, groups of 3: 678, then 345, then 12.
4. So 12345678 is 12,345,678: twelve million three hundred forty five thousand six hundred seventy eight.
Answer: Indian 1,23,45,678; American 12,345,678

content.publication_text: Show that a lakh is a hundred thousands, a crore a hundred lakhs and an arab a hundred crores. Then find the zeros in a thousand lakh and in a hundred thousand.

content.text:
$1$. A lakh: $100 \times 1000 = 1,00,000$, with $5$ zeros.
$2$. A crore: $100 \times 1,00,000 = 1,00,00,000$, with $7$ zeros.
$3$. An arab: $100 \times 1,00,00,000 = 1,00,00,00,000$, with $9$ zeros.
$4$. A thousand lakh: $1000 \times 1,00,000 = 10,00,00,000$, which has $8$ zeros and is ten crore.
$5$. A hundred thousand: $100 \times 1000 = 1,00,000$, which has $5$ zeros and is one lakh.
Answer: A thousand lakh has $8$ zeros; a hundred thousand has $5$ zeros
steps: A lakh: 100 × 1000 = 1,00,000, with 5 zeros.
A thousand lakh: 1000 × 1,00,000 = 10,00,00,000, which has 8 zeros and is ten crore.
A hundred thousand: 100 × 1000 = 1,00,000, which has 5 zeros and is one lakh.

media.description: Six numbers of seven to ten digits are cut into Indian groups and into American groups. Each is then read with its lakh, crore or arab names and with its million or billion names, and the commas are taken out again to check.

video_script.why: The child has placed commas in both systems and read a ten digit number, and now does the same for six numbers.

<bookmark mark='m3'/>The groups are one, zero one, zero one and zero one zero.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The third name is ten crore, twenty lakh, thirty thousand and forty.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, the second name is one billion, one million, one thousand and one.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>The groups are one, zero zero one, zero zero one and zero zero one.
Joined, they make one zero zero one zero zero one zero zero one.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Cut it the Indian way, three digits from the right and then twos.
The groups are one, zero zero, one zero, zero one and zero zero one.
We join the groups because the number is just the groups written in order.

<bookmark mark='m3'/>Cut the Indian way.
The groups are nine, zero eight, zero seven, zero zero and six zero zero.
We cut again, so the same digits get Indian commas.

An arab is a billion and ten lakh is a million, so it matches.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The last reads nine arab, eight crore, seven lakh, six hundred.
Eight crore is eighty million and seven lakh is seven hundred thousand, so it matches too.

media.title: Which number is bigger in each pair?
media.context: Large Numbers Around Us. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Four pairs of numbers, each given with a unit like thousand, lakh, million, crore or billion, are written in full and compared by their digits. Each pair is then checked by writing both numbers in the same unit.

video_script.why: The child knows the zeros in a thousand, lakh, crore, million and billion, and now uses them to compare numbers given with different units.

marks.m1: the small title card From your book appears
marks.m2: the four pairs appear, each with a blank box between its numbers
marks.m3: the first pair, 30 thousand and 3 lakhs, is lit
marks.m4: a question mark appears in the anchor band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Four pairs of numbers are given.
Compare and write less than, greater than or equal.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The first pair is thirty thousand and three lakhs.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Which of the two is bigger?

<bookmark mark='m2'/>A thousand has three zeros, a lakh has five, and a million has six.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A crore has seven zeros, and a billion has nine.

marks.m2: 3 × 1,00,000 = 3,00,000 is written with 6 digits counted

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, write both numbers of a pair in full.
Thirty times one thousand has five digits.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Three times one lakh has six digits.
Fewer digits means a smaller number, so thirty thousand is smaller.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Five hundred times one lakh has eight digits.
Five times one million has seven digits.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>More digits means a bigger number, so five hundred lakhs is bigger.

marks.m1: 800 × 1000 = 8,00,000 is written with 6 digits counted
marks.m2: 8 × 10,00,000 = 80,00,000 is written with 7 digits counted
marks.m3: 640 × 1,00,00,000 = 6,40,00,00,000 is written with 10 digits counted
marks.m4: 60 × 1,00,00,00,000 = 60,00,00,00,000 is written with 11 digits counted

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, in the next pair, eight hundred times one thousand has six digits.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Eight times one million has seven digits, so eight hundred thousand is smaller.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Six hundred forty times one crore has ten digits.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Sixty times one billion has eleven digits, so six hundred forty crore is smaller.

marks.m1: both numbers of each pair are rewritten in one unit
marks.m2: 300 thousand beside 30 thousand, and 50 lakhs beside 500 lakhs
marks.m3: 8 lakhs beside 80 lakhs, and 640 crore beside 6000 crore

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, check by writing both numbers of a pair in the same unit.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Three lakhs is three hundred thousand, which is more than thirty thousand.
Five million is fifty lakhs, which is less than five hundred lakhs.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Eight hundred thousand is eight lakhs, and eight million is eighty lakhs.
Sixty billion is six thousand crore, which is more than six hundred forty crore.
We use one unit because numbers in the same unit are easy to compare.
beats.on_screen: Step 3: check in one unit: 3 lakhs = 300 thousand, more than 30 thousand; 5 million = 50 lakhs, less than 500 lakhs; 800 thousand = 8 lakhs, 8 million = 80 lakhs; 60 billion = 6000 crore, more than 640 crore

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Each pair now has its sign.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Thirty thousand is less than three lakhs.
Five hundred lakhs is greater than five million.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Eight hundred thousand is less than eight million.
Six hundred forty crore is less than sixty billion.
beats.on_screen: Answer: 30 thousand < 3 lakhs; 500 lakhs > 5 million; 800 thousand < 8 million; 640 crore < 60 billion

never_show: a sign between the numbers of a pair before the answer beat
maths_rules: zeros: thousand 3, lakh 5, million 6, crore 7, billion 9
30 thousand = 30 × 1000 = 30,000 (5 digits); 3 lakhs = 3 × 1,00,000 = 3,00,000 (6 digits); fewer digits, so 30 thousand < 3 lakhs
800 thousand = 800 × 1000 = 8,00,000 (6 digits); 8 million = 8 × 10,00,000 = 80,00,000 (7 digits); so 800 thousand < 8 million
check in the same unit: 3 lakhs = 300 thousand > 30 thousand; 5 million = 50 lakhs < 500 lakhs; 800 thousand = 8 lakhs < 80 lakhs = 8 million; 60 billion = 6000 crore > 640 crore

video_script.wrong_move: Kiko rounds seven hundred thirty two to the nearest hundred and orders seven hundred sweets. Seven hundred is less than the number of people, so thirty two people would get none.
maths_rules: the school has 732 people, so at least 732 sweets are needed
ordering 750 sweets: 750 − 732 = 18 more than needed, so the approximate number is more than the actual number: rounding up
the item costs 470 and the shopkeeper says around 450: 470 − 450 = 20 less than the cost, so it is rounding down
500 would be 500 − 470 = 30 more than the cost, so 450 is nearer to 470
round up: food for a group; round down: the time left to catch a bus; either: the distance between two far away places; exact: money in a bank

topics.summary: A rounded value is enough when the size matters more than the exact count; rounding to a place looks at the digit to its right.

content.text:
1.4 Exact and Approximate Values
1 lakh people visited the book fair. "Ohh, so many people!" "If I had not gone, they would have written 99,999 people visited the book fair last week".
What do you think of this conversation? Have you read or heard such headlines or statements?
Very often, exact numbers are not required and just an approximation is sufficient. For example, according to the 2011 census, the population of Chintamani town is 76,068. Instead, saying that the population is about 75,000 is enough to give an idea of how big the quantity is.
Bappi, call and check if Toofan Express is on time. "What number did you call?" "I called the rounded off number, of course! My teacher told us that efficient people deal with rounded off numbers."
There are situations where it makes sense to round up a number (rounding up is when the approximated number is more than the actual number). For example, if a school has 732 people including students, teachers and staff: the principal might order 750 sweets instead of 700 sweets.
There are situations where it is better to round down (rounding down is when the approximated number is less than the actual number). For example, if the cost of an item is ₹470, the shopkeeper may say that the cost is around ₹450 instead of saying it is around ₹500.
Think and share situations where it is appropriate to (a) round up, (b) round down, (c) either rounding up or rounding down is okay and (d) when exact numbers are needed.

content.text:
Worked example: A school has 732 people and the principal orders sweets. An item costs 470 rupees and the shopkeeper says around 450 rupees. Which one rounds up and which rounds down? Give one situation for each of: round up, round down, either, exact.
1. 732 is more than 700, so an order of 700 sweets leaves 732 − 700 = 32 people without.
2. 750 is more than 732, so ordering 750 rounds up and every person gets a sweet.
3. 450 is less than 470, so saying around 450 rounds down; 470 − 450 = 20 rupees less.
4. Round up: buying food for a group. Round down: the time left to catch the school bus.
5. Either: the distance between two far away places. Exact: handling money in a bank.

content.question: A school has 732 people and the principal orders sweets. An item costs 470 rupees and the shopkeeper says around 450 rupees. Which one rounds up and which rounds down? Give one situation for each of: round up, round down, either, exact.
content.publication_text:
Worked example: A school has 732 people and the principal orders sweets. An item costs 470 rupees and the shopkeeper says around 450 rupees. Which one rounds up and which rounds down? Give one situation for each of: round up, round down, either, exact.
1. 732 is more than 700, so an order of 700 sweets leaves 732 − 700 = 32 people without.
2. 750 is more than 732, so ordering 750 rounds up and every person gets a sweet.
3. 450 is less than 470, so saying around 450 rounds down; 470 − 450 = 20 rupees less.
4. Round up: buying food for a group. Round down: the time left to catch the school bus.
5. Either: the distance between two far away places. Exact: handling money in a bank.
Answer: Ordering 750 rounds up; saying around 450 rounds down; the four situations are given above

content.publication_text: Find all numbers whose five nearest neighbours are all $5,00,00,000$, and say how many there are.

content.text:
$1$. The nearest thousand is the strictest: the number must be within half a thousand of $5,00,00,000$.
$2$. The smallest such number is $5,00,00,000 - 500 = 4,99,99,500$, which rounds up.
$3$. The largest is $5,00,00,000 + 499 = 5,00,00,499$, since $5,00,00,500$ rounds up to $5,00,01,000$.
$4$. Count: $5,00,00,499 - 4,99,99,500 + 1 = 1000$.
$5$. These numbers also round to $5,00,00,000$ at ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh and crore.
Answer: All numbers from $4,99,99,500$ to $5,00,00,499$; there are $1000$ of them

content.text:
Roxie and Estu are estimating the values of simple expressions.
1. 4,63,128 + 4,19,682. Roxie: "The sum is near 8,00,000 and is more than 8,00,000." Estu: "The sum is near 9,00,000 and is less than 9,00,000."
(a) Are these estimates correct? Whose estimate is closer to the sum?
(b) Will the sum be greater than 8,50,000 or less than 8,50,000? Why do you think so?
(c) Will the sum be greater than 8,83,128 or less than 8,83,128? Why do you think so?
(d) Exact value of 4,63,128 + 4,19,682 = ____

content.text:
1. Predict first: is the sum nearer to 8,00,000 or to 9,00,000?
2. Round each part, add, and decide whether the real sum is more or less by seeing which way each part was rounded.
3. Compare each part with a benchmark part: if both parts are bigger than the benchmark parts, the sum is bigger.

content.text:
$1$. Roxie rounds down both parts to $4,00,000 + 4,00,000 = 8,00,000$, so the sum is more than that.
$2$. Estu rounds up to $5,00,000 + 4,00,000 = 9,00,000$, so the sum is less than that. Both are correct.
$3$. The exact sum is $4,63,128 + 4,19,682 = 8,82,810$.
$4$. Distance from $9,00,000$: $9,00,000 - 8,82,810 = 17,190$. Distance from $8,00,000$: $8,82,810 - 8,00,000 = 82,810$. Estu is closer.
$5$. $4,63,128$ is more than $4,50,000$ and $4,19,682$ is more than $4,00,000$, so the sum is more than $8,50,000$.
$6$. $8,83,128$ is $4,63,128 + 4,20,000$. Since $4,19,682$ is less than $4,20,000$, the sum is less than $8,83,128$.
Answer: Both estimates are correct; Estu's is closer; more than $8,50,000$; less than $8,83,128$; exact sum $8,82,810$

$3$. The exact difference is $14,63,128 - 4,90,020 = 9,73,108$.
$4$. Distance from $10,00,000$: $10,00,000 - 9,73,108 = 26,892$. Distance from $9,00,000$: $9,73,108 - 9,00,000 = 73,108$. Roxie is closer.
$5$. $14,63,128$ is more than $14,50,000$ and $4,90,020$ is less than $5,00,000$, so the difference is more than $14,50,000 - 5,00,000 = 9,50,000$.
$6$. $9,63,128$ is $14,63,128 - 5,00,000$. Since $4,90,020$ is less than $5,00,000$, the difference is more than $9,63,128$.
Answer: Both estimates are correct; Roxie's is closer; more than $9,50,000$; more than $9,63,128$; exact difference $9,73,108$

4. Mumbai is the largest city in both years, and New Delhi is second.

content.text:
$1$. Pune in $2011$: $31,15,431$, which is about $31$ lakh. In $2001$: $25,38,473$, about $25$ lakh.
$2$. Approximate increase: $31$ lakh $- 25$ lakh $= 6$ lakh. The exact increase is $31,15,431 - 25,38,473 = 5,76,958$.
$3$. Look for large jumps: Bengaluru $84,25,970 - 43,01,326 = 41,24,644$.
$4$. Hyderabad grew by $31,72,487$, Ahmedabad by $20,50,500$ and Surat by $20,33,962$, all less than Bengaluru.
$5$. So Bengaluru grew the most, by $41,24,644$.
Answer: Pune: $31,15,431$ in $2011$, grew by about $6$ lakh. Bengaluru grew the most, by $41,24,644$

$1$. Bengaluru: about $43$ lakh in $2001$, twice is about $86$ lakh, and $2011$ is about $84$ lakh. Close to double.
$2$. Hyderabad: $36$ lakh doubled is $72$ lakh, and $2011$ is $68$ lakh. Surat: $24$ lakh doubled is $48$ lakh, and $2011$ is about $45$ lakh.
$3$. Vadodara: $17$ lakh doubled is $34$ lakh, and $2011$ is about $36$ lakh.
$4$. Ahmedabad with $55$ lakh against $70$ lakh and Pimpri-Chinchwad with $17$ lakh against $20$ lakh are not close.
$5$. Patna is about $17$ lakh and Mumbai is about $124$ lakh. Now $7 \times 17 = 119$ and $8 \times 17 = 136$, so about $7$.
$6$. Exact: $1,24,42,373 \div 16,84,222$ is about $7.39$.
Answer: Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Surat and Vadodara nearly doubled; multiply Patna's population by about $7.39$

media.title: Halve and Double
media.context: Class 7 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 1 'Large Numbers Around Us' (Patterns in Products). Halve one number, double another. The product stays the same. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Halve and Double. Halve one number, double another. The product stays the same. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: Halving one factor and doubling another keeps the product the same, and pairing factors that make 10, 100 or 1000 turns a long product into a single power of ten.
tool_config.title: Halve and Double
tool_config.screen: A product line of factors as cards; a halve button and a double button that act on two chosen cards; a pair button that merges two cards when their product is a power of ten; a running product box that stays equal.
feedback: A halve on an odd card is refused with a note to halve another card.
A pair that does not make a power of ten is separated again with its product shown.
The running product box shows the same value after every move so the idea of keeping it equal is seen.
tool_config.done_when: All six products are found by regrouping and the running product is the same at every step.

content.text:
1.5 Patterns in Products
Roxie and Estu are playing with multiplication. They encounter an interesting technique for multiplying a number by 10, 100, 1000, and so on.
A Multiplication Shortcut
Roxie evaluated 116 × 5 as follows: 116 × 5 = (116 × 10) ÷ 2 = 1160 ÷ 2 = 580.
Estu evaluated 824 × 25 as follows: 824 × 25 = (824 × 100) ÷ 4 = 82,400 ÷ 4 = 20,600.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 116 × 5 half of 116 × 10, or twice it?
2. 5 is 10 ÷ 2, so multiplying by 5 is multiplying by 10 and then halving.
3. 25 is 100 ÷ 4, so multiplying by 25 is multiplying by 100 and then dividing by 4.

content.text:
Worked example: Roxie finds 116 × 5 by multiplying by 10 and halving. Estu finds 824 × 25 by multiplying by 100 and dividing by 4. Do both.
1. 116 × 10 = 1160.
2. 1160 ÷ 2 = 580, so 116 × 5 = 580.
3. 824 × 100 = 82,400.
4. 82,400 ÷ 4 = 20,600, so 824 × 25 = 20,600.
Answer: 116 × 5 = 580 and 824 × 25 = 20,600

Worked example: Roxie finds 116 × 5 by multiplying by 10 and halving. Estu finds 824 × 25 by multiplying by 100 and dividing by 4. Do both.
1. 116 × 10 = 1160.
2. 1160 ÷ 2 = 580, so 116 × 5 = 580.
3. 824 × 100 = 82,400.
4. 82,400 ÷ 4 = 20,600, so 824 × 25 = 20,600.
Answer: 116 × 5 = 580 and 824 × 25 = 20,600

1. Predict first: 8 × 5 is how many groups of 5? How does that compare with 8 × 10?
2. Ten in each group is twice as many as five in each group, so 8 × 5 is half of 8 × 10.
3. Dividing by 2 and multiplying by 10 scales by 10 ÷ 2, which is 5.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students multiply 116 by 5 by multiplying by 10 and halving, and multiply 824 by 25 by multiplying by 100 and dividing by 4.
Students explain using the meaning of multiplication and division why multiplying by 5 matches multiplying by 10 and dividing by 2.
Students regroup the factors of a product into tens, hundreds and thousands by halving and doubling, and use the regrouping to find products quickly.

content.text: Explain why a number times $5$ is the number times $10$ divided by $2$, using $8 \times 5$.
content.question: Explain why a number times 5 is the number times 10 divided by 2, using 8 × 5.
content.question_tex: Explain why a number times $5$ is the number times $10$ divided by $2$, using $8 \times 5$.
content.publication_text: Explain why a number times $5$ is the number times $10$ divided by $2$, using $8 \times 5$.

content.text:
$1$. $8 \times 10$ means $8$ groups of $10$, which is $80$.
$2$. $5$ is half of $10$, so each group has half as many.
$3$. So $8 \times 5$ is half of $80$, which is $40$.
$4$. In general, $5 = 10 \div 2$, so $n \times 5 = (n \times 10) \div 2$.
$5$. Dividing first also works: $(8 \div 2) \times 10 = 40$.
Answer: $5 = 10 \div 2$, so times $5$ is times $10$ then halve, e.g. $8 \times 5 = 40$
steps: 8 × 10 means 8 groups of 10, which is 80.
5 is half of 10, so each group has half as many.
So 8 × 5 is half of 80, which is 40.
In general, 5 = 10 ÷ 2, so n × 5 = (n × 10) ÷ 2.
Dividing first also works: (8 ÷ 2) × 10 = 40.

media.context: Large Numbers Around Us. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Three products are found quickly by pairing numbers that make a hundred or a thousand, and by writing one hundred twenty five as a thousand divided by eight. Each answer is then checked by another route.

video_script.why: The child has seen times five as times ten then half, and now looks for pairs that make round numbers and for a factor that is a round number divided by something.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Find quick ways to calculate these products.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The first is two times one thousand seven hundred sixty eight times fifty.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The second is seventy two times one hundred twenty five.
The book hints that one hundred twenty five is one thousand divided by eight.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>The third is one hundred twenty five times forty times eight times twenty five.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>How can we calculate each one quickly?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Some pairs of numbers multiply to give a round number such as one hundred or one thousand.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two times fifty makes one hundred, and eight times one hundred twenty five makes one thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Forty times twenty five also makes one thousand, and multiplying by a round number only adds zeros.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>We work the same way as the shortcut examples in your book.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, in the first product, pair two with fifty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two times fifty makes one hundred.
What is left is one thousand seven hundred sixty eight times one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Two zeros join the end of the digits one seven six eight.

marks.m3: 72,000 is split as 64,000 and 8,000

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, in the second product, write one hundred twenty five as one thousand divided by eight.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Seventy two times one thousand is seventy two thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Divide seventy two thousand by eight in two parts, sixty four thousand and eight thousand.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Sixty four thousand divided by eight is eight thousand, and eight thousand divided by eight is one thousand.
We add the two parts.
We use the hint because a thousand is easy to multiply with.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, in the third product, pair one hundred twenty five with eight.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>Pair forty with twenty five, and that also makes one thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>What is left is one thousand times one thousand.
We pair them because each pair makes a round number.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check each answer by another route.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>For the first, two thousand times one hundred is a little more than our answer.
<bookmark mark='m2b'/>That is right, because one thousand seven hundred sixty eight is less than two thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>For the second, add one hundred twenty five times seventy and one hundred twenty five times two.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>That is eight thousand seven hundred fifty plus two hundred fifty, which agrees.
For the third, three zeros and three more zeros make six zeros in all.

media.title: How do we calculate these products quickly?
media.context: Large Numbers Around Us. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Four products of twenty five with twelve and with multiples of ten are found by making a hundred and by moving zeros, and a pair of numbers is found for a product of twelve crore. Each answer is then checked by another route.

video_script.why: The child has used times ten and times a hundred with halving and dividing, and now makes a hundred from twenty five and moves zeros between factors.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Calculate these products quickly.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The first is twenty five times twelve.
The second is twenty five times two hundred forty.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The third is two hundred fifty times one hundred twenty.
The fourth is two thousand five hundred times twelve.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>For the last one, we must find two numbers whose product is twelve crore.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>How can we calculate each of these without long multiplication?

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, for twenty five times twelve, write twelve as three times four.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twenty five times four makes one hundred, so the product is one hundred times three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>For twenty five times two hundred forty, write two hundred forty as twenty four times ten.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Twenty five times twenty four is one hundred times six.
Then the factor ten adds one zero at the end.

marks.m1: 250 is rewritten as 25 × 10 and 120 as 12 × 10
marks.m4: an arrow marks the result of 25 × 12 with two zeros added

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, two hundred fifty is twenty five times ten, and one hundred twenty is twelve times ten.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two hundred fifty times one hundred twenty equals twenty five times twelve, times one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Two thousand five hundred times twelve also equals twenty five times twelve, times one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Both take the result of the first product and add two zeros.
We move the zeros because the product stays the same.

marks.m1: 12 crore is written as 12 followed by 7 zeros
marks.m2: the 7 zeros are drawn as seven small circles
marks.m3: the circles are shared 2 and 5, then 3 and 4

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, twelve crore is twelve followed by seven zeros.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We can share the seven zeros between two numbers in many ways.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Give two zeros to twelve and five zeros to one.
Or give three zeros to twelve and four zeros to one.
We share the zeros because any split of seven zeros gives the same product.
beats.on_screen: Step 3: 12 crore = 12 followed by 7 zeros; share the 7 zeros: 12 with 2 zeros × 1 with 5 zeros, or 12 with 3 zeros × 1 with 4 zeros

marks.m1: the word check is written above four check lines
marks.m5: the third and fourth lines are marked with 2 zeros
marks.m6: 2 zeros + 5 zeros = 7 zeros and 3 zeros + 4 zeros = 7 zeros are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check each answer by another route.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twelve times twenty five is ten times twenty five plus two times twenty five.
That is two hundred fifty plus fifty.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Two hundred forty times twenty five is two hundred forty times one hundred, divided by four.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Twenty four thousand divided by four is five thousand plus one thousand, which agrees.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>The third and fourth both have two zeros after the digits of the first, so they agree.
<bookmark mark='m6'/>For the last one, two zeros and five zeros make seven zeros.
Three zeros and four zeros also make seven.
beats.on_screen: Step 4: check: 12 × 25 = 10 × 25 + 2 × 25 = 250 + 50; 240 × 25 = (240 × 100) ÷ 4 = 24,000 ÷ 4 = 5,000 + 1,000; the third and fourth each have 2 zeros after the digits of the first; 2 zeros + 5 zeros = 7 zeros and 3 zeros + 4 zeros = 7 zeros

marks.m2: the first four answers are lit one by one
marks.m3: the two example numbers for the blanks are lit

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Each product was found by making a hundred or by moving zeros.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The answers are three hundred, six thousand, thirty thousand and thirty thousand.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>For the last one, twelve hundred times one lakh is one example.

media.title: Digit Count Predictor
media.context: Class 7 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 1 'Large Numbers Around Us' (Patterns in Products). Predict how many digits a product has. Then check the smallest and the largest. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Digit Count Predictor. Predict how many digits a product has. Then check the smallest and the largest. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: An m-digit number times an n-digit number has m plus n digits or one fewer, and the smallest and largest numbers of those lengths show both cases.
tool_config.title: Digit Count Predictor
tool_config.screen: Two digit-count pickers for the factors; a predicted digit count the student sets; the smallest product and the largest product computed from the smallest and largest numbers of those lengths and shown with their digit counts; a free multiply box to test more pairs.
feedback: A prediction with the wrong count shows the smallest product beside it.
A tested pair that lies between the smallest and the largest is placed on a bar between them.
A correct answer states the rule with the two digit counts added.
tool_config.done_when: All six digit-count pairs are predicted correctly.

hint_ladder.text: Which numbers give the smallest product and the largest product?
Count the digits of the smallest product and of the largest product.
Compare with the sum of the two digit counts.
The smallest and largest products are shown with their digits, and the rule is read out; a new pair follows.

student_does: Predict the digit counts of the product before the tool shows it.
Pick the digit counts of the two numbers.
Read the digit counts of the smallest and largest products.
Try your own pair of numbers in the multiply box.

3. Use the pattern to jump to a longer multiplication, then check one of them with the usual method.

content.text:

content.text:
$1$. Smallest: $10 \times 10 = 100$, which has $3$ digits.
$2$. Largest: $99 \times 99 = 9801$, which has $4$ digits.
$3$. Every other product lies between them, so Roxie is right.
$4$. Two $3$-digit numbers: the smallest is $100 \times 100 = 10,000$, which already has $5$ digits. So never $4$ digits.
$5$. For a $4$-digit and a $2$-digit number: the smallest is $1000 \times 10 = 10,000$, which has $5$ digits, so yes.
$6$. The largest is $9999 \times 99 = 9,89,901$, which has $6$ digits.
Answer: Roxie is right; two $3$-digit numbers never give $4$ digits; a $4$-digit times a $2$-digit number can give $5$ digits or $6$ digits

concepts.concept_name: How Long is the Product?: Q3

content.text:
$1$. For a $1$-digit number times a $1$-digit number the counts are $1$ and $2$: $1 + 1 - 1 = 1$ and $1 + 1 = 2$.
$2$. Multiplying a $5$-digit number by a $5$-digit number gives $5 + 5 - 1 = 9$ or $5 + 5 = 10$ digits.
$3$. An $8$-digit number times a $3$-digit number gives $8 + 3 - 1 = 10$ or $8 + 3 = 11$ digits.
$4$. Multiplying a $12$-digit number by a $13$-digit number gives $12 + 13 - 1 = 24$ or $12 + 13 = 25$ digits.
$5$. Rule: an $m$-digit number times an $n$-digit number has $m + n - 1$ or $m + n$ digits.
Answer: $9$ or $10$; $10$ or $11$; $24$ or $25$ digits. The rule is $m + n - 1$ or $m + n$ digits

content.text:
Fascinating Facts about Large Numbers
Some interesting facts about large numbers are hidden below. Calculate the product or quotient to uncover the facts. Once you find the product or quotient, read the number in both Indian and American naming systems. Share your thoughts and questions about the fact with the class after you discover each number.
1250 × 380 is the number of kirtanas composed by Purandaradasa according to legends. Purandaradasa was a composer and singer in the 15th century. His kirtanas spanned social reform, bhakti and spirituality. He systematised methods for teaching Carnatic music which is followed to the present day. How many years did he live to compose so many songs? At what age did he start composing songs? If he composed 4,75,000 songs, how many songs per year did he have to compose?
2100 × 70,000 is the approximate distance in kilometres between the Earth and the Sun. This distance keeps varying throughout the year. The farthest distance is about 152 million kilometres. How did they measure the distance between the Earth and the Sun?
6400 × 62,500 is the average number of litres of water the Amazon river discharges into the Atlantic Ocean every second. The river's flow into the Atlantic is so much that drinkable freshwater is found even 160 kilometres into the open sea.

content.text:
As you did before, divide the given numbers to uncover interesting facts about division. Share your thoughts and questions with the class after you uncover each number.
13,95,000 ÷ 150 is the distance (in kms) of the longest single-train journey in the world. The train runs in Russia between Moscow and Vladivostok. The duration of this journey is about 7 days. The longest train route in India is from Dibrugarh in Assam to Kanyakumari in Tamil Nadu; it covers 4219 kms in about 76 hours.
Adult blue whales can weigh more than 10,50,00,000 ÷ 700 kilograms. A newborn blue whale weighs around 2,700 kg, which is similar to the weight of an adult hippopotamus. Blue whales can eat up to 3500 kg of krill every day.
52,00,00,00,000 ÷ 130 was the weight, in tonnes, of global plastic waste generated in the year 2021.
Large Number Fact: In a single gram of healthy soil there can be 100 million to 1 billion bacteria and 1 lakh to 1 million fungi, which can support plants' growth and health.
Share such large-number facts you know / come across with your class.

content.text:
$1$. $1250 \times 380 = 4,75,000$: four lakh seventy five thousand in the Indian system, and four hundred seventy five thousand in the American system.
$2$. $2100 \times 70,000 = 14,70,00,000$: fourteen crore seventy lakh, or one hundred forty seven million.
$3$. $6400 \times 62,500 = 40,00,00,000$: forty crore, or four hundred million.
$4$. To ask how long Purandaradasa composed, suppose he composed for $50$ years. Then $4,75,000 \div 50 = 9,500$ songs a year.
$5$. The Earth to Sun distance is about $14,70,00,000\text{ km}$, which is about $147$ million kilometres.
Answer: $4,75,000$; $14,70,00,000$; $40,00,00,000$ (named in both systems above)

topics.summary: A what-if question about a large number becomes a calculation once you state an assumption and work in stages.

content.text:
1.6 Did You Ever Wonder...?
Estu is amused by all these interesting facts about large numbers. He came up with an unusual question, "Could the entire population of Mumbai fit into 1 lakh buses?" What do you think? How can we find out?
Let us assume a bus can accommodate 50 people. Then 1 lakh buses can accommodate 1 lakh × 50 = 50 lakh people.
The population of Mumbai is more than 1 crore 24 lakhs (we saw this in an earlier table). So, the entire population of Mumbai cannot fit in 1 lakh buses.
The RMS Titanic ship carried about 2500 passengers. Can the population of Mumbai fit into 5000 such ships?

The population of Mumbai is more than 1 crore 24 lakhs (we saw this in an earlier table). So, the entire population of Mumbai cannot fit in 1 lakh buses.
The RMS Titanic ship carried about 2500 passengers. Can the population of Mumbai fit into 5000 such ships?

1. Predict first: one lakh buses of 50 people each. Is that more or less than one crore people?
2. State the assumption, multiply, and compare with the population of Mumbai.
3. A fit needs a capacity at least as big as the population.

content.text: Could Mumbai's population, $1,24,42,373$, fit into $1$ lakh buses of $50$ people each? Could it fit into $5000$ ships of $2500$ people each?
content.question: Could Mumbai's population, 1,24,42,373, fit into 1 lakh buses of 50 people each? Could it fit into 5000 ships of 2500 people each?
content.book_number: Did You Ever Wonder: Mumbai in buses and ships
content.question_tex: Could Mumbai's population, $1,24,42,373$, fit into $1$ lakh buses of $50$ people each? Could it fit into $5000$ ships of $2500$ people each?
content.publication_text: Could Mumbai's population, $1,24,42,373$, fit into $1$ lakh buses of $50$ people each? Could it fit into $5000$ ships of $2500$ people each?

content.text:
$1$. $1,00,000 \times 50 = 50,00,000$ people in the buses.
$2$. $50,00,000$ is less than $1,24,42,373$, so no.
$3$. $5000 \times 2500 = 1,25,00,000$ people in the ships.
$4$. $1,25,00,000 - 1,24,42,373 = 57,627$, so the ships have room for $57,627$ more people than the city.
$5$. So yes, $5000$ such ships could carry everyone.
Answer: No for the buses, as $50,00,000$ is too few; yes for the ships, as $1,25,00,000$ is more

5000 × 2500 = 1,25,00,000 people in the ships.
1,25,00,000 − 1,24,42,373 = 57,627, so the ships have room for 57,627 more people than the city.
So yes, 5000 such ships could carry everyone.

content.text: At $100\text{ km}$ a day, how far is a year and ten years, and can Roxie reach the Moon $(3,84,400\text{ km})$?

content.publication_text: At $100\text{ km}$ a day, how far is a year and ten years, and can Roxie reach the Moon $(3,84,400\text{ km})$?

content.text:
$1$. In a year: $100 \times 365 = 36,500\text{ km}$.
$2$. In ten years: $36,500 \times 10 = 3,65,000\text{ km}$.
$3$. $3,84,400 - 3,65,000 = 19,400$, so she is $19,400\text{ km}$ short of the Moon.
Answer: $36,500\text{ km}$ in a year; $3,65,000\text{ km}$ in $10$ years; $19,400\text{ km}$ short of the Moon

content.text: At $1000\text{ km}$ a day, can you reach the Sun, $14,70,00,000\text{ km}$ away, in a lifetime of $100$ years?
content.question: At 1000 km a day, can you reach the Sun, 14,70,00,000 km away, in a lifetime of 100 years?
content.book_number: Did You Ever Wonder: the Sun at 1000 km a day
content.question_tex: At $1000\text{ km}$ a day, can you reach the Sun, $14,70,00,000\text{ km}$ away, in a lifetime of $100$ years?
content.publication_text: At $1000\text{ km}$ a day, can you reach the Sun, $14,70,00,000\text{ km}$ away, in a lifetime of $100$ years?

content.text:
$1$. Days needed: $14,70,00,000 \div 1000 = 1,47,000$ days.
$2$. Days in $100$ years: $365 \times 100 = 36,500$, which is less than $1,47,000$.
$3$. Years needed: $1,47,000 \div 365$ is about $402.7$ years.
$4$. So no, a lifetime is not enough.
Answer: $1,47,000$ days, about $402.7$ years, so not in a lifetime
steps: Days in 100 years: 365 × 100 = 36,500, which is less than 1,47,000.

So no, a lifetime is not enough.

media.description: The ten digits zero to nine are used once each to make a ten digit number. The biggest digits go first for the largest multiple of five, and the smallest start with a small fix at the end gives the smallest even number. Each number is checked at the end.

Row 2 digits left to right, in columns 3 to 7: 8, 7, 6, 5, 4. Group 2 (lower), 0.7 below the last row of group 1: the tag 'Smallest difference' in INK, then row 1 digits 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4 and row 2 digits, in columns 3 to 7: 9, 9, 8, 8, 7. Every digit is centred in its box, drawn in ANSWER green, sans-serif, at least 34 px high on a 1920-px canvas. No sign between the rows and no total.

source: Grey-headed albatrosses have a roughly 7-feet wide wingspan. They are known to migrate across several oceans. Albatrosses can cover about 900 to 1000 km in a day. content.text: Using all digits from $0$ to $9$ exactly once (the first digit cannot be $0$) to create a $10$-digit number, write the $(a)$: largest multiple of $5$; $(b)$: smallest even number.
content.question: Using all digits from 0 to 9 exactly once (the first digit cannot be 0) to create a 10-digit number, write the (a) largest multiple of 5 (b) smallest even number.
content.question_tex: Using all digits from $0$ to $9$ exactly once (the first digit cannot be $0$) to create a $10$-digit number, write the $(a)$: largest multiple of $5$; $(b)$: smallest even number.
content.publication_text: Using all digits from $0$ to $9$ exactly once (the first digit cannot be $0$) to create a $10$-digit number, write the $(a)$: largest multiple of $5$; $(b)$: smallest even number.

content.text:
$1$. A multiple of $5$ ends in $0$ or $5$. For the largest, put the digits in the biggest order, which ends with $0$: $9876543210$.
$2$. An even number ends in an even digit. The smallest start is $1$, then $0$, then the other digits in order.
$3$. That order is $1023456789$, but it ends in $9$, which is odd.
$4$. Swap the last two digits to end with $8$: $1023456798$. This is the smallest even number.
Answer: $(a)$: $9876543210$; $(b)$: $1023456798$

content.text: The number $10,30,285$ in words is Ten lakhs thirty thousand two hundred eighty five, which has $42$ letters. Give a $7$-digit number name which has the maximum number of letters.
content.question: The number 10,30,285 in words is Ten lakhs thirty thousand two hundred eighty five, which has 42 letters. Give a 7-digit number name which has the maximum number of letters.
content.question_tex: The number $10,30,285$ in words is Ten lakhs thirty thousand two hundred eighty five, which has $42$ letters. Give a $7$-digit number name which has the maximum number of letters.
content.publication_text: The number $10,30,285$ in words is Ten lakhs thirty thousand two hundred eighty five, which has $42$ letters. Give a $7$-digit number name which has the maximum number of letters.

content.text:
$1$. Use the same style of naming as the book, with the plural in ten lakhs.
$2$. Choose the lakh digits, the thousand digits and the last three digits so that each part has a long word.
$3$. Seventy seven lakhs seventy seven thousand seven hundred seventy seven is $77,77,777$. It has $61$ letters.
$4$. Checking all $7$-digit numbers by computer gives $61$ as the maximum, reached by $81$ numbers; $73,73,373$ is the smallest of them.
Answer: The largest number of letters is $61$, for example $77,77,777$

content.text: Write a $9$-digit number where exchanging any two digits results in a bigger number. How many such numbers exist?
content.question: Write a 9-digit number where exchanging any two digits results in a bigger number. How many such numbers exist?
content.question_tex: Write a $9$-digit number where exchanging any two digits results in a bigger number. How many such numbers exist?
content.publication_text: Write a $9$-digit number where exchanging any two digits results in a bigger number. How many such numbers exist?

content.text:
$1$. Exchanging two digits makes the number bigger only if the smaller digit is on the left.
$2$. So every digit must be smaller than all the digits to its right: the digits increase from left to right.
$3$. The digits must be different, and zero cannot lead. The only choice is the nine digits $1$ to $9$ in increasing order.
$4$. So the number is $12,34,56,789$ and it is the only one.
Answer: $12,34,56,789$; exactly one such number

So the number is 1,23,45,67,89 and it is the only one.

content.text:
$1$. The number has $20$ digits, so $10$ digits remain.
$2$. Put the largest digit first. Strike out the four digits $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$ in front of the first $5$.

$4$. Two strikes remain. Strike out the next $1$ and $2$ so that $3$ comes next.
$5$. What remains is $5534512345$.
Answer: $5534512345$

content.text:
$1$. Write each number name and compare it with the next one.
$2$. Names like nineteen and twenty share $n$, $t$ and $e$. Ninety nine and one hundred share $n$ and $e$.
$3$. Checking every pair of neighbours up to three million, in the Indian and the international spelling, finds no pair without a shared letter.
$4$. So there may be no such pair at all; the search turns up none.
Answer: No such pair was found, however far we count

content.text: Suppose you write down all the numbers $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $\ldots$, $9$, $10$, $11$, ... content.text: How many lakhs make a billion?
content.question: How many lakhs make a billion?
content.question_tex: How many lakhs make a billion?

content.text:
$1$. A billion is $100$ crore, and a crore is $100$ lakh.
$2$. So a billion is $100 \times 100$ lakh $= 10,000$ lakh.
$3$. Check: $10,000 \times 1,00,000 = 1,00,00,00,000$, which is $1$ followed by $9$ zeros.
Answer: $10,000$ lakhs make a billion

content.text:
$1$. Somu's building is $40\text{ m}$ tall.
$2$. Eagles: $4500 \div 40 = 112.5$ and $6000 \div 40 = 150$. So about $112$ to $150$ times.
$3$. Mount Everest: $8850 \div 40 = 221.25$, so about $221$ times.
$4$. Aeroplanes: $10,000 \div 40 = 250$ and $12,800 \div 40 = 320$. So $250$ to $320$ times.
Answer: Eagles $112.5$ to $150$ times, Everest about $221$ times, aeroplanes $250$ to $320$ times

diagram_spec.manim_description: On a plain BG canvas draw the ten digits 0 to 9 built from straight sticks, in two rows of five that read left to right and then top to bottom: row 1 shows 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and row 2 shows 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Every digit sits in an invisible box 0.8 wide and 1.6 tall (box centre cx, cy). Box centres are 1.3 apart across a row: cx = -2.6, -1.3, 0, 1.3, 2.6; row 1 has cy = 1.5 and row 2 has cy = -1.5. The seven stick positions of a box are: a = top, from (cx-0.4, cy+0.8) to (cx+0.4, cy+0.8); b = upper right, from (cx+0.4, cy+0.8) to (cx+0.4, cy); c = lower right, from (cx+0.4, cy) to (cx+0.4, cy-0.8); d = bottom, from (cx-0.4, cy-0.8) to (cx+0.4, cy-0.8); e = lower left, from (cx-0.4, cy) to (cx-0.4, cy-0.8); f = upper left, from (cx-0.4, cy+0.8) to (cx-0.4, cy); g = middle, from (cx-0.4, cy) to (cx+0.4, cy). Draw only the lit sticks, each as a separate straight INK line of width 0.09 with round caps, shortened by 0.07 at both ends so that neighbouring sticks stay separate and countable; unlit positions stay empty. Sticks per digit: 0 = a b c d e f; 1 = b c; 2 = a b g e d; 3 = a b g c d; 4 = f g b c; 5 = a f g c d; 6 = a f g e c d; 7 = a b c (exactly three sticks); 8 = a b c d e f g; 9 = a b c d f g. Under each digit box, centred 0.4 below its bottom edge, write that digit as a numeral in INK sans-serif at least 34 px high on a 1920-px canvas. Every digit sits in an invisible box 0.8 wide and 1.6 tall (box centre cx, cy). Box centres are 1.3 apart across a row: cx = -2.6, -1.3, 0, 1.3, 2.6; row 1 has cy = 1.5 and row 2 has cy = -1.5. The seven stick positions of a box are: a = top, from (cx-0.4, cy+0.8) to (cx+0.4, cy+0.8); b = upper right, from (cx+0.4, cy+0.8) to (cx+0.4, cy); c = lower right, from (cx+0.4, cy) to (cx+0.4, cy-0.8); d = bottom, from (cx-0.4, cy-0.8) to (cx+0.4, cy-0.8); e = lower left, from (cx-0.4, cy) to (cx-0.4, cy-0.8); f = upper left, from (cx-0.4, cy+0.8) to (cx-0.4, cy); g = middle, from (cx-0.4, cy) to (cx+0.4, cy). media.description: An example, the biggest number and the smallest number are made with exactly twenty four sticks. content.text:
Toothpick Digits
We can write digits as shown in the image below. You can either use toothpicks or matchsticks, or just write the digits in this way, using lines to represent sticks.
To make the digit 7, three sticks are needed.
Write or make the number 5108. How many sticks are required?
1. Make or write the number 42,019. It would require exactly 23 sticks.
2. Starting with 42,019, add or write two more sticks, and make a bigger number. One example is 42,078. What other numbers bigger than 42,019 can you make in this way?

content.text:
1. The digits are drawn like a calculator display: 0 uses 6 sticks, 1 uses 2, 2 uses 5, 3 uses 5, 4 uses 4, 5 uses 5, 6 uses 6, 7 uses 3, 8 uses 7 and 9 uses 6.

content.text:
$1$. Example: $2008$ uses $5 + 6 + 6 + 7 = 24$ sticks.
$2$. Biggest: use the cheapest digit $1$ as many times as possible, $24 \div 2 = 12$ times, and $12$ digits make the longest number: $1,11,11,11,11,111$.
$3$. Smallest: three digits hold at most $3 \times 7 = 21$ sticks, which is under $24$, so four digits are needed.
$4$. The first digit should be as small as possible: $1$ uses $2$ sticks and leaves $22$, more than the $21$ that three digits can hold. The next choice is $2$ with $5$ sticks, leaving $19$, and $0$, $0$, $8$ uses $6 + 6 + 7 = 19$.
$5$. So the smallest is $2008$.
Answer: Example $2008$; biggest $1,11,11,11,11,111$; smallest $2008$

content.text:
Summary
We came across large numbers, lakhs, crores and arabs; millions and billions. We learnt how to read and write these numbers in the Indian and American/International naming systems.
(a) 1 lakh is 1 followed by 5 zeroes: 1,00,000
(b) 1 crore is 1 followed by 7 zeroes: 1,00,00,000
(c) 1 million is 1 followed by 6 zeroes: 1,000,000 (which is also ten lakhs)
(d) 1 arab is 1 followed by 9 zeroes: 1,000,000,000 (which is also 100 crore or 1 billion)
We generally round up or round down large numbers. Many times it is enough just to know roughly how big or small something is.
To get a sense of large numbers or quantities, we can check how many times bigger they are compared to numbers or quantities that are more familiar.
We saw how to factorise numbers and regroup them to make multiplications simpler.
We carried out interesting thought experiments such as, "Would one be able to watch 1000 movies in a year?"
